sentences: A third-order tensor decomposition expresses an array as a sum of rank-one outer products of three vector families.
Kruskal's theorem guarantees uniqueness when the three families' Kruskal ranks sum to at least twice the number of components plus two.
The question asks for an efficient decomposition algorithm throughout this uniqueness regime, including cases beyond linear independence of all components.
For a cubic tensor, these conditions can certify substantially more components than the dimension, where the familiar simultaneous-diagonalization approach no longer applies directly.
An algorithmic proof, especially a robust one, would connect identifiability of latent-variable models with practical recovery from estimated moments.

context_blocks.title: Identifiability and computation
context_blocks.text: The 2014 source asks for efficient decomposition of a third-order tensor throughout Kruskal's uniqueness regime, where the component families have Kruskal ranks satisfying \(k_a+k_b+k_c\ge 2R+2\). A unique decomposition need not come with an efficient recovery procedure.

context_blocks.title: Robustness and model scope
context_blocks.text: Page 3 also asks about algorithmic proofs of robust uniqueness statements, motivated by tensors estimated from samples. This remains sourced context: exact decomposition and stable recovery from noisy entries impose different guarantees. The field, finite input and output representation, running-time parameters, conditioning promises and accuracy dependence still need specification before this draft is a self-contained benchmark.
